docs.text: HardFOC driver AT25040 Driver ¶ A header-only C++17 driver for the Microchip AT25040B serial EEPROM (also AT25010B and AT25020B). It detects the chip safely, reads and writes it in pages and reports every result as a status, on any MCU with SPI. Quickstart API guide Source on GitHub The driver has no platform code. You give it a small class with one method that runs an SPI transaction; it does the rest: the instruction set, the ninth address bit, bounds and page checks, and a probe that tells a missing chip from a present one. 4-Kbit SPI serial EEPROM AT25040B Microchip (Atmel) Memory 512 x 8 bits (AT25040B); 128 x 8 (AT25010B), 256 x 8 (AT25020B); 8-byte pages Interface SPI mode 0 or 3, MSB first; 20 MHz at 4.5 V to 5.5 V, 10 MHz at 2.5 V, 5 MHz at 1.8 V Supply 1.8 V to 5.5 V; 3.5 µA maximum standby at 5 V Writes Self-timed, 5 ms maximum per page; 1,000,000 cycles, 100-year retention Protection WP pin, write-enable latch, block protection of the top ¼, top ½ or whole array Package 8-lead SOIC, TSSOP, UDFN, XDFN, 8-ball VFBGA; -40 °C to +85 °C Product page and datasheet What you get ¶ One object per chip. at25040::Device<YourSpi> with Probe() , Read() , Write() , WritePage() , WaitReady() , block protection and the write-enable latch. See API guide . Safe detection. Probe() reads the status register twice and rejects a floating bus ( 0xFF ) and a bus that echoes the command back. See Hardware . The ninth address bit handled. Addresses 0x100 to 0x1FF put A8 into the opcode for you. See Protocol . Checks before the bus. A bad pointer, a zero length, a range past the array or a write that crosses a page returns Status::Arg without touching SPI. Zero-overhead portability. The port is a CRTP class: no virtual calls, no heap, no exceptions, no RTOS. See Porting . Tested without hardware. Host unit tests run the driver against a model of the chip. See Testing and CI . docs.text: API guide ¶ How to do the common jobs with the driver: detect the chip, wait, read, write, protect and handle errors. Every snippet on this page is compiled by the host CI from tests/docs/api_tasks.cpp , with Eeprom standing for at25040::Device<MySpi> . The API reference lists every member. The shape of the API ¶ One at25040::Device<Spi> object per chip, constructed from a reference to your port. It is not copyable and holds no buffers beyond the stack frame of each call. Call What it does Probe() Two RDSR: decides whether a chip is fitted ReadStatus(sr) One RDSR: write-cycle polling, protection level Read(addr, dst, len) READ: any range inside the array, in transactions of up to 16 data bytes WritePage(addr, src, len) WREN + WRITE: 1 to 8 bytes in one page, then waits for the write cycle Write(addr, src, len) Any range inside the array: one WritePage() per 8-byte page WaitReady(timeout_ms) RDSR until RDY clears: the end of a write cycle (default 10 ms budget) WriteEnable() , WriteDisable() One WREN or WRDI: set or clear the write-enable latch SetBlockProtection(level) WREN + WRSR: BP1:BP0, then waits for the write cycle GetBlockProtection(level) One RDSR, decoded into at25040::BlockProtect LastRdsr() No transfer: the last status byte read, for logging Every call except LastRdsr() returns at25040::Status and never throws. Check it. During a write cycle the chip ignores every instruction except RDSR. Every call that sends one ( Read() , the writes, WriteEnable() , WriteDisable() , SetBlockProtection() ) therefore reads the status register first and returns Status::Busy , sending nothing else, when RDY is 1. The driver's own writes wait for their write cycle, so you see Busy only when something else started one: firmware reset in the middle of a write, or an instruction you sent through your port. Detect the chip ¶ bool attach ( Eeprom & eeprom ) { switch ( eeprom . Probe ()) { case at25040 :: Status :: Ok : return true ; case at25040 :: Status :: Busy : // a write cycle is still running: try again in 5 ms case at25040 :: Status :: Absent : // no chip, floating MISO, MISO echoing MOSI, or a write cycle // (0xFF) default : std :: printf ( "no AT25040 (RDSR 0x%02X) \n " , eeprom . LastRdsr ()); return false ; } } Call Probe() from an explicit attach or start-up step, not from a static constructor: the SPI bus may not be up yet. A write cycle in progress also reads as Absent (every status bit is 1 while busy), so probe before you write, or wait 5 ms after the last write. Protocol lists every decision. Wait for a write cycle ¶ After a WRITE or WRSR the chip runs an internal write cycle of up to 5 ms (t WC ) and ignores everything except RDSR until it is done. WritePage() and Write() wait for it before they return, so the next call is never ignored. WaitReady() is the same wait on its own: use it after an instruction you sent through your port, or at start-up, when the firmware may have been reset in the middle of a write: // After an MCU reset the chip may still be finishing a write the old firmware started. WaitReady() // polls RDSR until RDY clears (default budget 10 ms, twice the 5 ms tWC). bool start_up ( Eeprom & eeprom ) { return eeprom . WaitReady () == at25040 :: Status :: Ok && eeprom . Probe () == at25040 :: Status :: Ok ; } WaitReady() polls RDSR until RDY (bit 0) reads 0 and returns Timeout when the budget runs out, or BusError when a poll's transfer fails (default kWriteCycleTimeoutMs = 10 ms, twice t WC ). If your port has the optional delay_us() hook ( Porting ), the driver sleeps 100 µs between polls; without it, it polls back to back for a bounded count that lasts at least the budget even at 20 MHz. A floating MISO reads 0xFF , which looks like a write cycle that never ends: it also returns Timeout . Read ¶ // Read() streams any range inside the array; the driver splits it into READ transactions. at25040 :: Status read_settings ( Eeprom & eeprom , uint8_t ( & settings )[ 64 ]) { return eeprom . Read ( 0x100 , settings , sizeof ( settings )); // 0x100-0x13F, A8 set by the driver } Read() returns all len bytes. The chip increments the address after every byte, so one READ could stream the whole array; the driver sends one READ per 16 data bytes ( Device::kReadChunkBytes ) so that a port never sees more than 18 bytes, and sets A8 in each opcode for addresses 0x100 and up. A range that runs past 0x1FF is refused with Status::Arg before anything is sent: the chip would roll over to 0x000 . If a transfer fails part way, Read() returns BusError and dst holds the chunks read before it. Write ¶ // Write() splits the range at 8-byte page boundaries and waits for each page's write cycle. at25040 :: Status store_serial ( Eeprom & eeprom , const uint8_t ( & serial )[ 12 ]) { return eeprom . Write ( 0x0FC , serial , sizeof ( serial )); // pages 0x0F8, 0x100 and 0x108 } A page is 8 bytes on an 8-byte boundary ( kPageSizeBytes ). WritePage() refuses a write that would cross one, because the chip would wrap inside the page and overwrite its start; Write() splits a longer range at the page boundaries. Each page costs one write cycle, so writing the whole 512-byte array takes 64 cycles, at most 320 ms. If a page fails, Write() returns its status and the pages before it are written. Status and block protection ¶ void print_status ( Eeprom & eeprom ) { uint8_t sr = 0 ; if ( eeprom . ReadStatus ( sr ) != at25040 :: Status :: Ok ) { return ; } const unsigned bp = ( sr & ( at25040 :: kSrBp1 | at25040 :: kSrBp0 )) >> 2 ; // 0 none, 1 top 1/4, 2 top 1/2, 3 all std :: printf ( "busy=%d write-enabled=%d protect-level=%u \n " , ( sr & at25040 :: kSrWip ) != 0 , ( sr & at25040 :: kSrWel ) != 0 , bp ); } SetBlockProtection() sends WREN and WRSR and waits for the write cycle; GetBlockProtection() reads the level back: // Make the top half (0x100-0x1FF: board ID, calibration) read-only. WP must be high. bool lock_identity ( Eeprom & eeprom ) { at25040 :: BlockProtect level = at25040 :: BlockProtect :: None ; if ( eeprom . GetBlockProtection ( level ) == at25040 :: Status :: Ok && level == at25040 :: BlockProtect :: UpperHalf ) { return true ; // already locked } if ( eeprom . SetBlockProtection ( at25040 :: BlockProtect :: UpperHalf ) != at25040 :: Status :: Ok ) { return false ; // Busy, BusError, Timeout } // The chip ignores WRSR when WP is low, so read the level back. return eeprom . GetBlockProtection ( level ) == at25040 :: Status :: Ok && level == at25040 :: BlockProtect :: UpperHalf ; } at25040::BlockProtect BP1:BP0 Read-only addresses (AT25040B) None 00 None UpperQuarter 01 0x180 - 0x1FF UpperHalf 10 0x100 - 0x1FF All 11 0x000 - 0x1FF The bits are non-volatile. With WP low the chip ignores WRSR and SetBlockProtection() still returns Ok , so read the level back as above. A write to a protected address is ignored by the chip and still returns Ok from WritePage() : read back what matters. WriteDisable() sends WRDI, which clears the write-enable latch regardless of WP. The driver's writes set the latch themselves and the chip clears it at the end of every write cycle, so you need WRDI only after a WriteEnable() for an instruction you then decided not to send: // Clear the write-enable latch after a WREN you sent for your own instruction. void abandon_write ( Eeprom & eeprom ) { ( void ) eeprom . WriteDisable (); // WRDI; Busy if a write cycle is still running } Handle errors ¶ const char * describe ( at25040 :: Status st ) { switch ( st ) { case at25040 :: Status :: Ok : return "ok" ; case at25040 :: Status :: Timeout : return "write cycle did not end in time" ; case at25040 :: Status :: BusError : return "SPI transfer failed" ; case at25040 :: Status :: Absent : return "no chip answered" ; case at25040 :: Status :: Busy : return "write cycle in progress, try again" ; case at25040 :: Status :: Arg : return "bad pointer, length or address" ; } return "unknown" ; } Status Meaning Ok The transactions completed. It does not prove a write was stored BusError Your port's transfer() returned false : the frame was not clocked (SPI driver error, bus lock timeout) Timeout A write cycle did not end within the WaitReady() budget (RDY still 1; also a floating MISO) Absent Probe() only: the bus answered, but with no plausible status register ( Protocol ). A failed transfer is BusError , not Absent Busy RDSR showed a write cycle in progress, so the call sent nothing else; try again after WaitReady() . From Probe() : RDY set in a status byte that is not 0xFF Arg Read() , WritePage() , Write() , SetBlockProtection() : null pointer, a level outside BlockProtect , zero length, range past the array, or a page crossing (nothing is sent) The chip itself reports nothing about a refused write (WP low, latch clear, protected block). The only check is to read the data back after the write cycle.

docs.text: Architecture ¶ How the driver is put together: three layers, what each owns, and how one call reaches the chip. Three layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your application talks to one at25040::Device object, whose public member functions (listed from inc/at25040.hpp) turn a call into AT25040 instructions: RDSR, WREN, READ and WRITE with A8 in the opcode. The communication interface (at25040::SpiInterface in inc/at25040_spi_interface.hpp) is a CRTP contract with one method. The platform port is the only code you write: a class whose transfer() runs one SPI transaction with chip select held low, and optionally delay_us() for the write-cycle wait. Below it is the hardware. Drawn from: inc/at25040.hpp Device members ; inc/at25040_spi_interface.hpp SpiInterface ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . The three layers ¶ Layer Where You change it Hardware-agnostic core : Device<Spi> , uses only the port's transfer() inc/at25040.hpp , inc/at25040_registers.hpp Never, for a new board Communication interface : SpiInterface<Derived> , one method inc/at25040_spi_interface.hpp Never Platform port : your class, on your SDK Your project Once per MCU or board ( Porting ) Everything above the port is the same on ESP32, STM32, a Linux host or the unit-test model. That is how the host tests run the real driver code without hardware. How one call reaches the chip ¶ sequenceDiagram participant A as Application participant D as Device participant P as Your port participant E as AT25040B A->>D: WritePage(0x110, data, 4) D->>D: check pointer, length, page and range D->>P: transfer([0x06], 1 byte) P->>E: WREN D->>P: transfer([0x0A, 0x10, d0..d3], 6 bytes) P->>E: WRITE, A8 in the opcode P-->>D: true loop until RDY = 0 (at most 10 ms) D->>P: transfer([0x05, 0x00], 2 bytes) P->>E: RDSR D->>P: delay_us(100), if the port has it end D-->>A: Status::Ok (write cycle finished) Each transfer() is one CS-low period, and the driver passes a 20 ms timeout to every transfer. Reads and status calls are one transfer per 16 data bytes; writes add the status polls of the write cycle. Why CRTP ¶ The interface is a class template parameter, not a virtual base class. The compiler sees your port's transfer() (and delay_us() , if it has one, detected at compile time) directly and inlines it; the driver has no vtable, allocates nothing and needs no RTTI. The cost is that the driver type names the port: Device<MySpi> . Code that has to work with several port types takes the driver as a template parameter too. Bounded waits, no hidden state ¶ The driver keeps one byte of state: the last status register value ( LastRdsr() ). It does not track the write cycle, the write-enable latch or the protection level; the chip does, and ReadStatus() reads them. The only wait is the write cycle: a write returns when RDSR shows the chip ready again, or with Timeout after kWriteCycleTimeoutMs (10 ms). docs.text: The interface is a class template parameter, not a virtual base class. The compiler sees your port's transfer() (and delay_us() , if it has one, detected at compile time) directly and inlines it; the driver has no vtable, allocates nothing and needs no RTTI. The cost is that the driver type names the port: Device<MySpi> . Code that has to work with several port types takes the driver as a template parameter too.
docs.title: Why CRTP

docs.text: The driver keeps one byte of state: the last status register value ( LastRdsr() ). It does not track the write cycle, the write-enable latch or the protection level; the chip does, and ReadStatus() reads them. The only wait is the write cycle: a write returns when RDSR shows the chip ready again, or with Timeout after kWriteCycleTimeoutMs (10 ms).

Changed ¶ BREAKING (behaviour): Read() , WritePage() , Write() , WriteEnable() , WriteDisable() and SetBlockProtection() read the status register first and return Status::Busy without sending anything else while a write cycle runs; the chip would ignore the instruction. docs.text: Configuration ¶ What you choose for an AT25040B: the part, the bus, write protection and the driver's fixed limits. The driver has no run-time configuration structure. Everything below is a board decision, a compile-time constant in inc/at25040_registers.hpp or a value in the chip's status register. Board decisions ¶ Decision Options Where it shows Part AT25010B (128 B), AT25020B (256 B), AT25040B (512 B) Address range you may use ( Hardware ) SPI clock 5, 10 or 20 MHz maximum, by VCC Your port's bus setup SPI mode 0 or 3 Your port's bus setup WP Tied high, or a GPIO Hardware write protection of the whole chip HOLD Tied high Must not float Constants ¶ Constant Value Meaning kCapacityBytes 512 Upper bound for Read() and WritePage() ranges kPageSizeBytes 8 Largest write, and the boundary a write may not cross kAddrA8Mask 0x08 Bit of the READ / WRITE opcode that carries A8 kCmdWren ... kCmdWrite 0x06 , 0x04 , 0x05 , 0x01 , 0x03 , 0x02 Instructions ( Protocol ) kSrWip , kSrWel , kSrBp0 , kSrBp1 0x01 , 0x02 , 0x04 , 0x08 Status register bits Limits inside Device : Constant Value Meaning (transfer timeout) 20 ms timeout_ms passed to every transfer() Device::kReadChunkBytes 16 Data bytes per READ transaction; Read() splits longer reads Device::kWriteCycleTimeoutMs 10 Default WaitReady() budget, used by every write: twice the 5 ms t WC Device::kPollIntervalUs 100 Sleep between status polls when the port has delay_us() Device::kPollsPerMsWithoutDelay 1112 Polls per millisecond of budget without delay_us() (one RDSR is 0.9 µs at 20 MHz) Block protection ¶ The protection level is stored in the chip (BP1:BP0, non-volatile) and survives power cycles. Set it once in production with SetBlockProtection() , as the API guide shows, and read it at start-up with GetBlockProtection() if your firmware depends on it. docs.text: Hardware ¶ What to connect between your MCU and an AT25040B, with which bus settings, and the board-level details that decide whether writes stick. All values here come from the AT25010B/AT25020B/AT25040B datasheet (Atmel-8707F, 01/2015). When they disagree with a board's schematic, the schematic wins for pin numbers. Pins ¶ The 8-lead SOIC and TSSOP use the same pin numbers; the 8-pad UDFN / XDFN and the 8-ball VFBGA number the same functions 1 to 8. Pin Signal Notes 1 CS, in Active low; each instruction starts on its falling edge 2 SO, out MISO; high impedance while CS is high 3 WP, in Active low; low blocks every write 4 GND 5 SI, in MOSI 6 SCK, in Clock 7 HOLD, in Active low; pauses a transfer 8 VCC 1.8 V to 5.5 V The driver does not drive WP or HOLD. Tie HOLD high. Tie WP high to allow writes, or drive it from a GPIO and hold it low to make the whole chip read-only in hardware. Bus settings ¶ Setting Value Mode 0 or 3, MSB first f SCK max 20 MHz (VCC ≥ 4.5 V), 10 MHz (≥ 2.5 V), 5 MHz (≥ 1.8 V) t CSS , t CSH , t CS min 100 ns (VCC ≥ 2.5 V), 200 ns (≥ 1.8 V) Frame Instruction, address (READ, WRITE), data; no dummy bytes t WC max 5 ms, self-timed, from the CS rising edge t CSS is CS setup before the first clock, t CSH CS hold after the last, t CS the CS high time between instructions. sequenceDiagram participant H as Host (driver) participant E as AT25040B H->>E: WREN 0x06 (CS low, 1 byte, CS high) H->>E: WRITE 0x0A (A8 = 1), address byte 0x10, 4 data bytes: address 0x110 Note over E: CS high: internal write cycle starts, 5 ms max H->>E: RDSR 0x05 E-->>H: 0xFF (busy: every status bit reads 1) H->>E: RDSR 0x05 E-->>H: 0x00 (ready, write-enable latch cleared) H->>E: READ 0x0B (A8 = 1), address byte 0x10 E-->>H: 4 data bytes The opcode carries the ninth address bit (A8) in bit 3 for READ and WRITE on the AT25040B. The driver sets it for addresses 0x100 to 0x1FF . Protocol has every instruction and the status register. Power ¶ Quantity Value VCC 1.8 V to 5.5 V; the clock limit depends on it Active current (5 V) 10 mA max at 20 MHz (read), 3 mA max at 1 MHz Standby current (max, CS high) 0.5 µA at 1.8 V, 1 µA at 2.5 V, 3.5 µA at 5 V Temperature -40 °C to +85 °C (industrial grade, H) Match VCC to the MCU's I/O voltage: the inputs need V IH of at least 0.7 x VCC. Decouple VCC with 100 nF close to pin 8. Write protection ¶ Three mechanisms stop a write; all of them make WritePage() and SetBlockProtection() look successful while nothing is stored, because the chip does not report a refused write. Mechanism Effect WP pin low (board) Every write and WREN is ignored Write-enable latch clear (power-up, WRDI / WriteDisable() , end of every write cycle) The next WRITE is ignored; WritePage() sends WREN first Block protection BP1:BP0 (WRSR / SetBlockProtection() , non-volatile) 01 : 0x180 - 0x1FF , 10 : 0x100 - 0x1FF , 11 : all read-only API guide shows how to read and set the protection level. Sharing the bus ¶ SO is high impedance whenever CS is high, so the AT25040B can share SCK, MOSI and MISO with other SPI devices on its own chip select. On the Flux analog front-end it sits on the ADS7952 bus as the second device. Variants ¶ Part Size Protected by BP = 01 / 10 AT25010B 128 x 8 0x60 - 0x7F / 0x40 - 0x7F AT25020B 256 x 8 0xC0 - 0xFF / 0x80 - 0xFF AT25040B 512 x 8, A8 in the opcode 0x180 - 0x1FF / 0x100 - 0x1FF BP = 11 protects the whole array on every part. The driver checks addresses against 512 bytes ( kCapacityBytes ). On the smaller parts, keep addresses below 128 or 256 yourself: the chip ignores the upper address bits, so higher addresses alias the start of the array. docs.text: Installation ¶ Add the driver to a CMake or ESP-IDF project. It is a header-only C++17 library with no dependencies. Requirements ¶ A C++17 compiler: GCC 7+, Clang 5+ or a current MSVC. No RTOS, heap or exceptions: every call is noexcept and returns at25040::Status . Get the source ¶ A git submodule keeps the driver pinned to a version you chose: git submodule add https://github.com/hardfoc/hf-at25040-driver.git external/hf-at25040-driver git submodule update --init external/hf-at25040-driver Only inc/ , cmake/ and CMakeLists.txt are needed to build. The examples have their own submodule ( examples/esp32/scripts ); you do not need it to use the driver. CMake ¶ add_subdirectory ( external/hf-at25040-driver ) target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE hf_at25040 ) # or the alias hf::at25040 hf_at25040 is an INTERFACE target: it carries the include directories ( inc/ and the generated version header) and requires C++17 ( cxx_std_17 ), so your target does not need to set either. Option Default Effect HF_AT25040_BUILD_TESTS OFF Builds the host unit tests and the documentation snippets in tests/ ( Testing and CI ) Installed package ¶ cmake --install copies the headers ( at25040.hpp , at25040_registers.hpp , at25040_spi_interface.hpp and the generated at25040_version.h ) to include/ and a CMake package to lib/cmake/hf_at25040/ , which provides the same target name as the build tree: cmake -S external/hf-at25040-driver -B build-at25040 cmake --install build-at25040 --prefix /opt/hardfoc find_package ( hf_at25040 CONFIG REQUIRED ) # CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/opt/hardfoc target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE hf::at25040 ) Without CMake, add inc/ to the include path. at25040.hpp then falls back to a built-in version string. ESP-IDF ¶ The ESP-IDF component wrapper is examples/esp32/components/hf_at25040/ . Copy that folder into your project's components/ (or point EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS at it) and set the HF_AT25040_ROOT cache variable to the driver checkout; the wrapper stops with a clear message when the path is wrong. Your component then declares REQUIRES hf_at25040 . Inside hf-core ¶ In the HardFOC core, the driver is a submodule of hf-core-drivers and is switched on with HF_CORE_ENABLE_AT25040 , which also compiles the At25040Handler : set ( HF_CORE_ENABLE_AT25040 ON ) include ( "${HF_CORE_DRIVER_EXT}/hf-at25040-driver/cmake/hf_at25040_build_settings.cmake" ) How the build is organised ¶ Layer File Role Settings cmake/hf_at25040_build_settings.cmake Target name, include directories, version: the single source of truth Library CMakeLists.txt INTERFACE target for host builds and CI, install and hf::at25040 export ESP-IDF examples/esp32/components/hf_at25040/CMakeLists.txt IDF component wrapper over the same settings The version is set once in the settings file and written into at25040_version.h at configure time. Read it at run time: const char * v = at25040 :: GetAt25040DriverVersion (); // "1.0.0" Next ¶ Quickstart wires the chip and stores a few bytes; Porting writes the SPI interface for your MCU.

docs.text: Porting ¶ Run the driver on a new MCU by writing one class with one method, the SPI transfer, and optionally a delay. The driver never calls your SDK directly. It calls transfer() on a class you derive from at25040::SpiInterface<Self> (in inc/at25040_spi_interface.hpp ). The base class uses CRTP: the call is resolved at compile time, so there are no virtual functions, no vtable and nothing to allocate. Three layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your application talks to one at25040::Device object, whose public member functions (listed from inc/at25040.hpp) turn a call into AT25040 instructions: RDSR, WREN, READ and WRITE with A8 in the opcode. The communication interface (at25040::SpiInterface in inc/at25040_spi_interface.hpp) is a CRTP contract with one method. The platform port is the only code you write: a class whose transfer() runs one SPI transaction with chip select held low, and optionally delay_us() for the write-cycle wait. Below it is the hardware. Drawn from: inc/at25040.hpp Device members ; inc/at25040_spi_interface.hpp SpiInterface ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . What you implement ¶ bool transfer ( const uint8_t * tx , uint8_t * rx , std :: size_t len , uint32_t timeout_ms ); Argument Contract tx , len Send len bytes in one transaction, CS low for all of them rx Receive len bytes: rx[i] is the byte clocked in while tx[i] went out timeout_ms Give up after this long and return false return true when the transaction completed, false on a bus error or timeout The driver always passes rx of the same length as tx (at most 18 bytes) and timeout_ms = 20 . SPI port ¶ my_spi.hpp #include "at25040_spi_interface.hpp" class MySpi : public at25040 :: SpiInterface < MySpi > { public : // One transaction: CS low, `len` bytes full duplex (SPI mode 0 or 3, MSB first), CS high. // rx[i] is the byte clocked in while tx[i] went out. Return false only on a bus error or timeout. bool transfer ( const uint8_t * tx , uint8_t * rx , std :: size_t len , uint32_t timeout_ms ) noexcept { return platform_spi_transfer ( tx , rx , len , timeout_ms ); } // Optional: sleep at least `us` microseconds. With it, WaitReady() (and every write) sleeps 100 // us between status polls; without it, the driver polls back to back for a bounded count. void delay_us ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } }; Rules the transfer must follow: SPI mode 0 or 3 , MSB first, no faster than the chip allows at your VCC: 20 MHz at 4.5 V, 10 MHz at 2.5 V, 5 MHz at 1.8 V. One transaction per call. CS goes low before the first byte and high after the last; never split a call into two CS periods, never merge two calls. The chip starts a write cycle on the CS rising edge after WRITE. Full duplex. Fill rx with what came back on MISO; Probe() and Read() read their results from it. Return false only for a bus failure. A missing chip is the driver's job: it shows up as 0xFF bytes. Optional delay hook ¶ void delay_us ( uint32_t us ); // sleep at least us microseconds The driver detects this member at compile time. With it, WaitReady() (and so every write) sleeps 100 µs between status polls; an RTOS port can yield there. Without it, the driver polls back to back for a bounded number of polls ( kPollsPerMsWithoutDelay per millisecond of budget) that lasts at least the budget even at 20 MHz, so a write still waits for its write cycle, but keeps the bus busy while it does. Chip select and shared buses ¶ Drive CS from the SPI peripheral (ESP-IDF spics_io_num , STM32 hardware NSS) or toggle a GPIO around the transfer. On a shared bus, take the bus lock for the whole transfer() so another device cannot get between CS low and CS high. Keep t CSS , t CSH and t CS at 100 ns or more (200 ns at 1.8 V). Reference implementation ¶ The ESP32 example's port in at25040_esp32_example.cpp is a complete ESP-IDF spi_master port: one spi_transaction_t with length = len * 8 , tx_buffer = tx and rx_buffer = rx , sent with spi_device_polling_transmit() on a device configured for mode 0 with CS on spics_io_num , and delay_us() on esp_rom_delay_us() . It does not use the ESP-IDF command or address phases: the driver puts the opcode (with A8 in bit 3) in tx[0] and the address byte in tx[1] . Check your port ¶ Build it: the port on this page is compiled by the host CI from tests/docs/ , with the driver instantiated over it. Call Probe() and log LastRdsr() . A ready AT25040B with no protection reads 0x00 ; 0xFF means nothing answered. Write one page ( WritePage() waits for the write cycle), read it back. Read across 0x0FF / 0x100 in two calls to prove A8 reaches the chip: the two halves must hold different data. Threads ¶ The driver is not thread-safe. Give each EEPROM one owner task, or guard every call on a driver object (and its port) with one mutex. On a shared bus, the bus lock in transfer() is not enough for a write followed by a status poll; hold the mutex for the whole sequence.

docs.text: Protocol ¶ The AT25040B's instruction set, status register and addressing, and which driver call uses each instruction. Every instruction starts with CS going low and ends with CS going high. Bytes go MSB first. An invalid opcode leaves SO in high impedance until the next CS falling edge. Instructions ¶ Instruction Opcode What it does WREN 0x06 Sets the write-enable latch; WP must be high. WriteEnable() , WritePage() , SetBlockProtection() WRDI 0x04 Clears the write-enable latch, regardless of WP. WriteDisable() RDSR 0x05 Reads the status register, also during a write cycle. ReadStatus() , Probe() , WaitReady() , GetBlockProtection() , and the busy check before every other instruction WRSR 0x01 Writes BP1:BP0 (non-volatile, takes a write cycle). SetBlockProtection() READ 0x03 , 0x0B with A8 Address byte, then data out; the address increments. Read() WRITE 0x02 , 0x0A with A8 Address byte, then 1 to 8 data bytes in one page. WritePage() The datasheet writes the opcodes as 0000 X110 (WREN) to 0000 A010 (WRITE); the constants are kCmdWren , kCmdWrdi , kCmdRdsr , kCmdWrsr , kCmdRead and kCmdWrite . A is address bit A8 on the AT25040B ( kAddrA8Mask = 0x08 ); X is ignored. During a write cycle every instruction except RDSR is ignored, so the driver sends RDSR first and returns Status::Busy instead of an instruction the chip would drop. Status register ¶ Bit Name Meaning 0 RDY ( kSrWip ) 1: write cycle in progress 1 WEN ( kSrWel ) 1: write-enable latch set 2 BP0 ( kSrBp0 ) Block protection, low bit 3 BP1 ( kSrBp1 ) Block protection, high bit 7:4 0 when ready During an internal write cycle all eight bits read 1, so a busy chip returns 0xFF . A ready chip returns 0x0X : only the low four bits can be set. Addressing and wrap-around ¶ READ : the address increments after each byte and rolls over from 0x1FF to 0x000 . WRITE : only the low three address bits increment, so a write wraps inside its 8-byte page and overwrites the start of the page. The driver never lets either wrap happen: Read() refuses a range past 0x1FF , WritePage() refuses a write that crosses a page, both with Status::Arg . Probe ¶ Probe() sends RDSR twice and decides from the two status bytes: Status bytes Result Typical cause A transfer failed BusError Bus error in the port The two bytes differ Absent Noise, a contended MISO 0xFF Absent Nothing drives MISO (pull-up or floating), or a write cycle is running 0x05 Absent MISO follows MOSI one byte late: the RDSR opcode comes back RDY set, not 0xFF Busy Not seen on an AT25040B, which reads 0xFF while busy Anything else Ok A ready chip: 0x00 to 0x0E LastRdsr() returns the first status byte of the last probe, for logging. A chip in its write cycle and a floating MISO both read 0xFF , so Probe() cannot tell them apart; call WaitReady() first when a write may still be running (after an MCU reset).

Wire it ¶ MCU AT25040B pin Notes SPI SCLK SCK (6) Mode 0 or 3; start at 1 MHz SPI MOSI SI (5) SPI MISO SO (2) High impedance while CS is high GPIO or hardware CS CS (1) Active low; one transaction per CS-low period 3.3 V (1.8 V to 5.5 V) VCC (8) Decouple with 100 nF close to the pin 3.3 V or GPIO WP (3) High to allow writes; low blocks every write 3.3 V HOLD (7) Keep high unless you pause transfers GND GND (4) Common ground with the MCU The Hardware page has the bus timing, the other packages and the protection options. 2. Add the driver ¶ Add the repository as a submodule and link the hf_at25040 CMake target (or add inc/ to your include path and build with C++17). Installation covers CMake and ESP-IDF. git submodule add https://github.com/hardfoc/hf-at25040-driver.git external/hf-at25040-driver 3. Write the port ¶ The port is the only platform code: one method that runs one SPI transaction. Replace the platform_* call with your SDK's. my_spi.hpp #include "at25040_spi_interface.hpp" class MySpi : public at25040 :: SpiInterface < MySpi > { public : // One transaction: CS low, `len` bytes full duplex (SPI mode 0 or 3, MSB first), CS high. // rx[i] is the byte clocked in while tx[i] went out. Return false only on a bus error or timeout. bool transfer ( const uint8_t * tx , uint8_t * rx , std :: size_t len , uint32_t timeout_ms ) noexcept { return platform_spi_transfer ( tx , rx , len , timeout_ms ); } // Optional: sleep at least `us` microseconds. With it, WaitReady() (and every write) sleeps 100 // us between status polls; without it, the driver polls back to back for a bounded count. void delay_us ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } }; Porting explains the contract and shows how to check a port. 4. Store and read back ¶ main.cpp #include "at25040.hpp" int store_and_read_back ( MySpi & spi ) { at25040 :: Device < MySpi > eeprom ( spi ); if ( eeprom . Probe () != at25040 :: Status :: Ok ) { // 1. a chip is there and idle return -1 ; // wiring, CS, power or SPI mode } const uint8_t serial [ 4 ] = { 0x12 , 0x34 , 0x56 , 0x78 }; if ( eeprom . WritePage ( 0x010 , serial , sizeof ( serial )) != at25040 :: Status :: Ok ) { // 2. one page, return -2 ; // 3. and its write cycle: WritePage() returns when the chip is ready again } uint8_t back [ 4 ] = {}; // 4. read it back if ( eeprom . Read ( 0x010 , back , sizeof ( back )) != at25040 :: Status :: Ok ) { return -4 ; } return back [ 0 ] == serial [ 0 ] ? 0 : -5 ; } What each step does: Probe() reads the status register twice. It returns Ok only when both reads agree, look like a real status byte and show no write in progress. WritePage() sends WREN, then WRITE with the address and up to eight bytes inside one page. The chip starts its internal write cycle when CS goes high. WritePage() then polls the status register until bit 0 (RDY) clears, at most 10 ms: during the write cycle the chip ignores everything except RDSR. Read() sends READ and the address and returns the bytes asked for, from any range inside the array. This example is built by the host CI, so it compiles against the current headers. If it does not work ¶ Symptom First thing to check Probe() returns Absent , LastRdsr() is 0xFF MISO wiring, CS reaching pin 1, VCC; a write cycle still running Probe() returns Absent , LastRdsr() is 0x05 MISO is connected to MOSI, or the wrong CS is low Writes return Ok but the data does not change WP is low, the address is block-protected, or you read before the write cycle ended Data at 0x100 and up appears at 0x000 The part is an AT25010B or AT25020B, not an AT25040B Troubleshooting has the full list. docs.text: Testing and CI ¶ How the driver is checked: host unit tests against a model of the chip, compiled documentation, ESP32 builds and static analysis, on every pull request. Host unit tests ¶ The tests build the real driver against a model of the AT25040B on the SPI bus: the instruction set with A8 in the opcode, the write-enable latch, page wrap-around, block protection, and a timed write cycle during which the status register reads 0xFF and every other instruction is ignored. Each transfer takes model time at the bus clock, and a second model adds the optional delay_us() hook. The bus can also float, echo MOSI or fail. cmake -S . -B build-host -DHF_AT25040_BUILD_TESTS = ON cmake --build build-host ctest --test-dir build-host --output-on-failure File Covers tests/test_device.cpp Probe decisions, A8 placement, argument checks, reads of any length across A8, page writes, multi-page Write() , waiting for the write cycle with and without a delay hook, wait timeouts, Busy before every instruction during a write cycle, WRDI and block protection tests/mock_at25040.hpp The chip model tests/install_consumer.cmake cmake --install into the build tree, then a find_package(hf_at25040) consumer that links hf::at25040 and includes every public header Documentation snippets ¶ Every C++ block on this site is included from tests/docs/ , which the host build compiles (target hf_at25040_doc_snippets ) with the driver instantiated over the documented port. docs.text: Troubleshooting ¶ Symptoms you may see while bringing up an AT25040B, their causes and the fix for each. Start with LastRdsr() after a failed Probe() : it tells a dead bus ( 0xFF ), a looped-back bus ( 0x05 ) and a working chip apart without a logic analyser. Symptom Cause and fix Probe() returns Absent , LastRdsr() is 0xFF Nothing drives MISO: wiring, CS on the wrong pin, no VCC. Fix: Check SO (pin 2) to MISO, CS (pin 1), VCC (pin 8) Same, right after an MCU reset The chip is finishing a write cycle the old firmware started: all status bits read 1. Fix: Call WaitReady() before Probe() Probe() returns Absent , LastRdsr() is 0x05 MISO echoes MOSI one byte late. Fix: Look for a short between SI and SO, or a missing device on that CS Probe() returns Absent , the two reads differ Bus contention or noise. Fix: Another device drives MISO while this CS is low; lower the clock Calls return Busy RDSR shows a write cycle in progress: one started outside the driver (an MCU reset during a write, a WRITE or WRSR sent through your port). Fix: WaitReady() , then retry Read() and the writes return Busy , Probe() returns Absent with 0xFF Nothing drives MISO, which then reads RDY = 1. Fix: Check SO (pin 2), CS (pin 1), VCC SetBlockProtection() returns Ok , GetBlockProtection() shows the old level WP is low: the chip ignores WRSR. Fix: WP (pin 3) high Every call returns BusError Your port's transfer() returned false . Fix: Bus not initialised, or the bus lock timed out WritePage() returns Ok , data unchanged WP low or the address is block-protected: the chip ignores the write. Fix: WP (pin 3) high; ReadStatus() BP bits WritePage() or WaitReady() returns Timeout , other calls work RDY still 1 after 10 ms: MISO reads 0xFF (floating), or the chip is damaged. Fix: Check SO (pin 2) and VCC; LastRdsr() shows the last status byte WritePage() returns Arg More than 8 bytes, or the write crosses an 8-byte page. Fix: Use Write() , which splits at page boundaries ( API guide ) Read() returns Arg Null buffer, zero length, or addr + len past 0x200 . Fix: Keep the range inside the array Data at 0x100 and up appears at 0x000 An AT25010B or AT25020B: no A8. Fix: Check the part marking; keep to its size Reads fine, writes fail at high clock Clock above the limit for your VCC. Fix: 5 MHz at 1.8 V, 10 MHz at 2.5 V, 20 MHz at 4.5 V Random failures, worse with long wires HOLD floating. Fix: Tie HOLD (pin 7) high
